sentences.text: Historical drawings show the bird had greyish or brownish feathers with a curly tuft on its rear, a naked grey head, and a beak colored green, black, and yellow.
Subfossil remains indicate the animal stood approximately 62.6 to 75 cm tall and weighed between 10.6 and 17.5 kg.
Today, a dried head is the only remaining soft tissue of the species.
Dutch sailors first recorded the bird in 1598, when Vice admiral Wybrand van Warwijck noted it in his journal under the name 'Walghvoghel'.
The last widely accepted sighting of the dodo occurred in 1662.
American geneticist Beth Shapiro and colleagues conducted the first DNA analysis of the dodo in 2002.
The bird used gizzard stones to digest food thought to include fruits while living in the woods of drier coastal areas of Mauritius.
It belongs to a clade of pigeons that are generally ground-dwelling and endemic to islands, evolving flightlessness and large size due to the lack of competing mammalian herbivores.
One account states that the dodo's clutch consisted of a single egg.
The dodo and the Rodrigues solitaire formed the subtribe Raphina, which belongs to the family Columbidae, a placement confirmed by genetic analysis.
Osteological and DNA analysis led to the dissolution of the family Raphidae, placing the dodo in the subfamily Raphinae and tribe Raphini.
The Nicobar pigeon is considered the closest living relative of the dodo based on genetic evidence.

Genetic studies suggest the ancestors of the dodo diverged from other lineages approximately 23.03 million years ago, long before the Mascarene Islands, where it lived, formed as volcanic islands less than 10 million years ago.

The dodo's exact appearance in life and its behavior remain unresolved due to varying portraits and limited evidence from live specimens, while there is ongoing scientific controversy regarding the accurate weight estimates of the dodo. The origin of the name 'dodo' is debated, with theories ranging from the Dutch word for 'sluggard' to 'Dodaars,' meaning 'fat-arse' or 'knot-arse.' It is now believed that the existence of a white dodo on Réunion was a confusion with the Réunion ibis and paintings.
